Predictive Validity of Loneliness and Misfit

We examined the predictive validity of loneliness and misfit for three political outcomes: populist voting intentions, electoral abstention, and populist attitudes. For each outcome, we estimated single-predictor models and an additive model including both predictors simultaneously. Logistic regression was used for populist voting intention (1 = populist party,0 = non-populist party) and voting abstention (1 = abstention,0 = voting intention). Linear regression was used for populist attitudes (Studies 1 and 2 only). Note that age and gender were included as covariates in supplementary analyses. However, their inclusion did not substantially alter the direction or significance of the loneliness and misfit effects reported below (see Supplementary Tables S9.1-S9.3).

Populist Voting Intention.

As single predictors, both loneliness and misfit were associated with populist voting intention in Studies 1 and 3, but not in Study 2. In the additive models, loneliness did not retain its predictive validity in any study, whereas misfit had a unique effect in Study 3 (Table 5, Figure 1).

Voting Abstention.

Loneliness and misfit each predicted voting abstention in Study 1, while only misfit did so in Study 3. Neither was significant in Study 2. In the additive models, misfit retained its predictive validity in Studies 1 and 3, whereas loneliness did not independently predict voting abstention in any study (Table 6, Figure 1). Populist Attitudes. Both loneliness and misfit predicted populist attitudes as single predictors in Studies 1 and 2. Again, when both constructs were added to the model, only misfit and not loneliness retained significant predictive power (Table 7, Figure 1). Discussion

We examined whether loneliness and misfit, a form of cultural estrangement capturing a perceived misalignment with mainstream society, constitute empirically distinct constructs and whether they display differential predictive validity for populist voting intention, voting abstention, and populist attitudes. Across three studies, we found that loneliness and misfit are related but empirically distinguishable constructs. While misfit retained a clear, constructspecific profile in bifactor analysis, loneliness was largely subsumed by a broader general factor shared with misfit. Regarding their predictive validity, both constructs were associated with populist voting intention, voting abstention, and populist attitudes when considered individually in most studies, yet once entered simultaneously, loneliness lost its predictive power in every model, while misfit retained a significant, independent effect in most cases.

These findings suggest that previously reported associations between loneliness and political outcomes may partly reflect variance shared with related constructs of social disconnection such as misfit, underscoring the need to conceptually and empirically disentangle such constructs in order to clarify their specific relevance for sociopolitical outcomes.

That loneliness and misfit, as an expression of alienation (Cozzarelli & Karafa, 1998), are empirically related aligns with the notion that both constructs tap into broader perceptions of social disconnection (Langenkamp, 2025). This may further be reflected in their shared empirical variance as shown by a general factor. Inspection of item content offers a possible substantive account for this pattern: loneliness items were, with few exceptions, more strongly associated with the general factor than with the loneliness-specific factor, suggesting that most of what loneliness captures is shared with misfit, plausibly a generalized sense of not belonging or fitting in with one's social surroundings. The few items retaining comparatively higher specific loadings (e.g., "There are people I can turn to," "There are people I can talk to") point to a narrower facet concerned with the availability of specific, trusted others as the main source of loneliness's residual unique variance, more closely aligned with the notion of emotional loneliness (Cacioppo et al., 2015; Weiss, 1973). Misfit items, by contrast, consistently retained higher specific than general loadings, indicating a more clearly delineated construct only partially accounted for by the shared general factor.

The conceptual undercurrent of items empirical distinction may lie in the different levels of social organization each construct refers to, with loneliness pertaining to interpersonal relationships and misfit to society at large. A similar distinction is drawn by Huxhold and colleagues (2022), who examined the empirical separability of loneliness, measured via the RTLS, and perceived social exclusion from society (e.g., "I feel like I do not really belong to society," "I feel excluded from society"; Bude & Lantermann, 2006). The authors similarly concluded that loneliness and social exclusion are related but empirically distinct, based on the different levels of social organization they pertain to. Whether misfit and perceived social exclusion, as operationalized in that study, are empirically distinct or merely two labels for one underlying phenomenon has yet to be tested.

On a conceptual note, misfit's societal-level focus is partially reminiscent of the collective facet of loneliness-the perceived absence of group-based affiliation with larger social groups or society at large grounded in shared norms or symbolic membership, which remains underrepresented in existing measures (Cacioppo et al., 2015; Hawkley et al., 2005 Hawkley et al., , 2012;; Maes et al., 2022). Misfit's emphasis on perceived divergence in values and opinions from the mainstream may reflect one particular route through which such collective nonaffiliation is experienced. Future work should develop an organizing framework that clarifies whether loneliness, misfit, and adjacent constructs relate hierarchically, as facets nested within broader constructs, or horizontally, as distinct but related forms of social disconnection, while guarding against the jingle-jangle fallacy (Kelley, 1927)-the same label concealing different constructs, or different labels concealing the same one.

Our results suggest that the distinction between loneliness and misfit is not merely psychometric but carries differential predictive validity for political outcomes. When examined as single predictors, both constructs were positively associated with populist voting intention, voting abstention, and populist attitudes in the majority of samples, consistent with the broader literature linking social disconnection to political disengagement and populist sympathies (Langenkamp, 2021b (Langenkamp, , 2021a;; Langenkamp & Bienstman, 2022; Neu et al., 2023; Peterson et al., 2025; Sanderson et al., 2019). When entered additively, however, misfit was the only predictor retaining significance in most of the samples. Because our data are only cross-sectional, this attenuation of loneliness is consistent with several causal interpretations:

First, perceived misfit may act as an upstream confounder that simultaneously impairs interpersonal relationships and drives political disaffection. Second, misfit may serve as a downstream mediator translating interpersonal isolation into broader cultural estrangement, meaning that controlling for misfit partitions away loneliness's indirect effect. Third, antiestablishment views may instead generate perceived misfit and subsequent social isolation, or unmeasured third variables (such as perceived marginalization) may jointly drive all three.

For example, societal or political arrangements involving exclusion and discrimination may drive populist voting and contribute to both loneliness and disaffection from mainstream politics alike (Barreto et al., 2024; Magnet & Orr, 2022; Tietjen, 2025). Finally, sample selection and attention-check exclusions may introduce collider bias if lonely, anti-system respondents are less likely to complete surveys attentively, artificially attenuating loneliness's direct link to political outcomes.

Based on our data, we cannot firmly conclude what explains our differential findings.

To us, in particular, the downstream mediator hypothesis is deserving of detailed attention:

Plausibly, misfit may be more proximal to sociopolitical attitudes and behavioral intentions due to its stronger emphasis on disconnection from the societal fabric rather than from interpersonal relationships. Tentative support for this account comes from a preprint that investigated differential associations of perceived disconnection from society at large (there termed perceived social marginalization) and from interpersonal relationships (i.e., loneliness, measured by the UCLA-LS short scale (Klein et al., 2021) with antifeminist attitudes (Langenkamp et al., preprint) that observe a similar pattern to our data. While we acknowledge that antifeminist and populist attitudes substantively differ, both have been conceptualized as 'thin ideologies' that juxtapose a valued collective against forces perceived as threatening it (Birsl, 2021; Höcker et al., 2025; Mudde, 2004), offering a cautiously relevant parallel to the present findings. Langenkamp and colleagues (preprint) found that perceived social marginalization showed a stronger association with antifeminist attitudes than loneliness when both were entered as joint predictors in one model. The dissociation reported there, however, was considerably weaker than observed in the present studies, with both predictors remaining significant.

However, the picture might be even more complicated than that misfit is a downstream mediator of the connection of loneliness to populist voting, attitudes and electoral abstention.

Several additional pathways have been proposed in the literature, primarily theorized with respect to loneliness. Loneliness has been associated with reduced interpersonal trustworthiness beliefs (Bellucci & Park, 2024; Langenkamp, 2023), poorer emotion regulation (Cacioppo & Hawkley, 2009), a more anxious and self-preservation-focused mindset, hypervigilance to social threats (Morr et al., 2022; Spithoven et al., 2017), and avoidance and withdrawal tendencies (Qualter et al., 2015; Spithoven et al., 2017).

Furthermore, individuals who perceive a loss of personal significance following social rejection appear more inclined to pursue extreme means of reclaiming social standing (Jasko et al., 2017), and alienation has similarly been linked to a stronger pull toward radical narratives (Bélanger et al., 2019). These psychological characteristics may increase vulnerability to populist narratives that cultivate distrust, provide simple solutions, and offer a strong sense of social belonging and identity (e.g., Bierwiaczonek et al., 2024; Jolley et al., 2023; Langenkamp & Bienstman, 2022; Peterson et al., 2025), or decrease the probability of political participation and weaken the perception of electoral participation as a civic duty (Langenkamp, 2021b (Langenkamp, , 2021a)). The nomological net that produces the empirical pattern might thus be difficult to disentangle. Notwithstanding these caveats, the observed empirical pattern rules out several prominent explanations for the connections of loneliness to populist voting, attitudes and electoral abstention. Most notably, the data contradicts theoretical models in which interpersonal loneliness directly drives populist attitudes, populist voting, or abstention independently of misfit, as well as models treating misfit merely as a politically inert side effect of loneliness. Likewise, any reverse-causal process could not operate solely through loneliness without directly affecting perceived misfit.

Our study has several limitations. First, both populist voting and voting abstention intentions were computed dichotomously, with only a small percentage of participants falling into these categories, limiting the generalizability of our findings and underscoring the need for more representative samples of political behavioral intentions and attitudes in future studies. Second, the cross-sectional nature of our data limits our capacity to rule out many plausible causal mechanisms that could drive the connection between loneliness, misfit and populist voting, attitudes and electoral abstention. Third, a wide range of concepts pertaining to social disconnection remain unexplored in this study; disentangling these constructs from loneliness, both conceptually and methodologically, remains an important task for future research (Huxhold et al., 2022). Relatedly, we chose the UCLA-LS as one of the most commonly used scales, but other measures better reflecting loneliness's proposed dimensional structure should be considered or developed in future work. Fourth, given the diversity of experiences encompassing perceived social disconnection, it may be important to include third variables at both the individual level (e.g., rejection sensitivity, Heu, 2025) and the macro level (e.g., digital infrastructure, Swader & Moraru, 2023; economic and welfare state characteristics, Nyqvist et al., 2019) that may moderate their relationship with political attitudes and behaviors (Langenkamp, 2025). Fifth, as in most previous studies, we assessed only voting intentions, leaving open whether actual voting behavior corresponds with our findings (Manunta et al., 2022; Langenkamp & Bienstman, 2022; Peterson et al., 2025).

In conclusion, given the scarcity of data comparing interpersonal and societal-level disconnection in their predictive power for populist attitudes, future, hopefully longitudinal, studies should more broadly test what conceptually and methodologically underlies the differential findings between loneliness and misfit, systematically considering further constructs pertaining to perceived social disconnection at different levels of social organization or additional distinguishing criteria.

Notwithstanding its plethora of limitations our study contributes novel data to the growing research linking measures of social disconnection to political behavior and attitudes.

By shedding light on the empirical distinction between loneliness and misfit and their differential relationship with populist attitudes, populist voting intentions, and abstention, the results suggest that perceived disconnection from society at large may hold greater predictive power for the measured political outcomes than interpersonal loneliness. Further research is needed to clarify the conceptual and methodological relationship between loneliness, misfit, and additional adjacent constructs not examined here, and to converge on an organizing framework for delineating and assessing these constructs.
